title: Bamboo Scaffolding: A Hong Kong Tradition at Risk
titleLines: A Hong Kong Tradition at Risk
paragraphs: Bamboo scaffolding has long been part of Hong Kong’s skyline, wrapping buildings like woven cages in midair.
For over 2,000 years, workers have used this technique for construction, festivals, and even theater stages. It’s fast, flexible, and uniquely tied to the city’s identity.

But that tradition may be fading. A new government rule now requires metal scaffolding for public housing projects over 15 meters tall, citing safety concerns after a rise in fatal falls and accidents in recent years. Officials say metal structures are easier to inspect, more stable in storms, and closer to international safety standards.

For many, though, the rule feels like the beginning of the end for bamboo. With fewer young workers entering the trade, and stricter requirements for inspections, training, and certification, some fear the centuries-old craft will slowly disappear from the city’s skyline. As one scaffolder put it: “It’s not just about building. It’s about passing on something that belongs to Hong Kong.”
